Part I: Data science in the messy middle

Set up the first part of the class: what data science is, where this course sits, and why AI is now impossible to ignore.

Suggested pacing: less than 1 minute.

Data science begins with a question

Data science is the study of data in order to understand something, decide something, or build something.

The code matters—but it is one link in a longer chain of choices.

Invite two or three quick student answers: What counts as data science? Then offer this deliberately broad definition. Emphasize that the goal is not code for its own sake.

Suggested pacing: 3 minutes.

[Sources] - /Users/aiwei/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Teaching/INST447/2025 Fall/Week 1 Introduction.pdf [/Sources]

Data has a lifecycle

Question→Data→Analysis→Explanation or decision↺

At every arrow, somebody makes a decision.

Use a familiar example such as choosing a restaurant, studying transit delays, or evaluating a public program. The lifecycle repeats: an answer normally creates a better next question.

Suggested pacing: 3 minutes.

[Sources] - /Users/aiwei/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Teaching/INST447/2025 Fall/Week 1 Introduction.pdf [/Sources]

A data pipeline is a sequence of decisions

Define→Locate→Acquire→Inspect + clean→Transform + combine→Analyze→Communicate

A result is only as trustworthy as the choices that produced it.

Walk left to right. Each stage can fail while still producing code that runs: the wrong dataset, a misunderstood field, an accidental row loss, or a misleading summary.

Suggested pacing: 3 minutes.

[Sources] - /Users/aiwei/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Teaching/INST447/2025 Fall/Week 1 Introduction.pdf [/Sources]

INST447 lives in the messy middle

You start with a question

Goals, constraints, and real-world context

→

You need a credible answer

Analysis, decisions, and communication

Between the question and the answer is the messy middle: locate, acquire, inspect, clean, reshape, combine, and validate data. That is this course.

This is the core course position. Students may have seen analysis or visualization before. Here we concentrate on the work that makes analysis possible and credible.

Suggested pacing: 3 minutes.

The lessons from 2025 still hold

  1. Taste and judgment matter. The tool cannot decide what “good” means for your situation.
  2. Complexity accumulates quietly. It gets easy to lose track of a large generated codebase.
  3. The tool amplifies your skill. Programming and data knowledge make it easier to specify, debug, and review.

Keep the original three lessons, but update the language. “Taste” includes knowing what outcome is useful, what tradeoff is acceptable, and what result is plausible.

Suggested pacing: 3 minutes.

[Sources] - /Users/aiwei/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Teaching/INST447/2025 Fall/Week 1 Introduction.pdf [/Sources]

AI goes beyond suggesting the next line

Coding assistant Coding agent
Works mainly in the current file or chat Inspects a repository and its instructions
Suggests code for you to place Edits files and runs commands
Waits for each next prompt Iterates through several steps
You execute and inspect each change You review the plan, evidence, and diff

The center of gravity moves from typing toward specifying, steering, and verifying.

Explain that this is a spectrum, not two sealed categories. Current tools may read files, edit code, run tests or other commands, and return a diff or summary for review. Do not dwell on brands; focus on the changed work pattern.

Suggested pacing: 3 minutes.

[Sources] - https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/cloud - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/how-claude-code-works - https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/github-copilot-app/managing-issues-and-pull-requests [/Sources]

Agentic coding is a loop, not a single prompt

State a goal→Inspect context→Plan→Edit→Run + check→Report evidence

Human gate: accept, redirect, investigate, or stop.

Compare this loop with the data pipeline. Both require explicit goals, evidence, and checking. The agent can take several actions, but the human still controls the acceptance decision.

Suggested pacing: 3 minutes.

[Sources] - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/how-claude-code-works - https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/code-review [/Sources]

What did the human contribute across those rounds?

Before and during

  • Describing the goal
  • Choosing constraints and priorities
  • Clarifying what the agent misunderstood

After each round

  • Testing the output
  • Noticing defects and awkward behavior
  • Deciding what to keep, change, or reject

Some people talk about token maximization: spend as many AI tokens as possible and ship whatever comes back. What is wrong with that? Tokens do not replace judgment.

Invite students to name other hidden human tasks. The list describes the human contribution across the rounds; do not imply that each item was included in the reported two hours of typing time. Connect this to data work: deciding whether a merge is correct, whether a missing value is meaningful, and whether a plot tells the truth.

Suggested pacing: 3 minutes.

[Sources] - Instructor-reported personal example supplied September 3, 2026. [/Sources]

More autonomy creates more ways to be wrong

A program can run and still…

  • answer the wrong question
  • discard the wrong rows
  • leak information across train and test data
  • encode a false assumption

An agent can also…

  • edit beyond the intended scope
  • trust a weak test
  • expose a credential
  • make many wrong changes quickly

The point is not fear. It is calibration. Automation increases both reach and blast radius. A green check is evidence about one condition, not proof that the analysis is correct.

Suggested pacing: 3 minutes.

[Sources] - https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/code-review - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/security [/Sources]

What you remain responsible for when AI writes code

Your responsibility Example
Understand the task and the data Explain what one row represents and what the code should output.
Read and make a small change Adjust a filter or selected field using an example and documentation.
Run validation and sanity checks Compare row counts before and after a join; inspect missing values and duplicates.
Protect data, keys, and the integrity of your submission Keep API keys out of notebooks and never upload private data without permission.

This condenses the six-item proposed minimum in the course-design working memory into four teachable responsibilities with examples. Do not present it as a newly adopted formal learning outcome, assessment policy, or closed-book requirement. The intended division of labor is simple: the tool can draft and execute; the student must be able to inspect, check, and explain.

Suggested pacing: 5 minutes.

[Sources] - /Users/aiwei/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Teaching/INST447/2026 Fall/week01_course_design_v1.md [/Sources]

A useful division of labor

AI can help

  • brainstorm approaches
  • draft or modify code
  • explain unfamiliar syntax
  • run repetitive checks
  • surface possible problems

You remain accountable

  • define the question
  • understand the data
  • choose what evidence matters
  • verify the result
  • explain what you submit

AI tools are welcome. Responsibility does not transfer to the tool.

This is the course-level message Wei has already been teaching in practice. It is not being elevated here into a new explicit course learning outcome. Invite one or two examples of where the boundary might be difficult.

Suggested pacing: 3 minutes.

[Sources] - /Users/aiwei/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Teaching/INST447/2026 Fall/week01_course_design_v1.md - /Users/aiwei/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Teaching/INST447/2026 Fall/week01_syllabus_v1.qmd [/Sources]

How does that affect our professional career?

Experience can compound

Senior developers often have more context for decomposition, tradeoffs, debugging, and review—so capable tools can amplify that judgment.

Practice can disappear

If agents absorb junior-shaped implementation tasks, newcomers may lose some of the repetition through which they would have built that judgment.

Early evidence points to pressure on young workers in AI-exposed jobs, but productivity effects vary sharply by task and context.

Answer the implicit question directly: the original claim remains plausible and important, but it should not be presented as universal or settled. Stanford’s revised 2026 working paper finds a widening employment gap for workers ages 22–25 in AI-exposed occupations, driven mainly by reduced hiring, while carefully calling the result descriptive rather than causal. Meanwhile, controlled studies of coding tools reach very different productivity results in different settings. The durable educational response is to preserve deliberate practice in specification, reading, debugging, checking, and explanation.

Suggested pacing: 4 minutes.

[Sources] - https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/publication/canaries-in-the-coal-mine-six-facts-about-the-recent-employment-effects-of-artificial-intelligence/ - https://metr.org/Early_2025_AI_Experienced_OS_Devs_Study-paper.pdf - https://github.blog/news-insights/research/research-quantifying-github-copilots-impact-on-developer-productivity-and-happiness/ [/Sources]

In 447, we should embrace AI at three levels

  1. AI as a coding assistant — draft, debug, and explain code.
    • “How could I change the name of this column?”
    • “How could I pivot the DataFrame into this format?”
  2. AI as a data processor — use an LLM through an API for structured extraction or augmentation.
    • “Extract the named entities (people, places, etc.) in each tweet of this dataset.”
    • “Augment this congress-speech dataset with the NYT headline of the day.”
  3. AI as an analysis pipeline — brainstorm, plan, and audit an end-to-end workflow.

Access matters: no paid AI subscription, or paid API is required for required course work. AI coding assistance is not required for completing programming assignments.

Free resources available to you: TerpAI (UMD), Gemini Education (UMD Google account), and Google AI Studio (free-tier API).

Retain the three levels from 2025 while updating “coding assistant” to include agentic work. Stress that every required lab and assignment is doable without AI. Students may use TerpAI, Gemini Education, and comparable tools, subject to the instructions for an activity.

Suggested pacing: 3 minutes.

Part III: Work that can be retraced

This final section is deliberately available as over-preparation. If the earlier discussion runs long, cover the pipeline and notebook-versus-script slides, then leave the directory example for students to review afterward.

Suggested pacing: less than 1 minute.

Use a workspace that makes the work visible

Notebooks are useful for

  • exploration
  • immediate output
  • narrative and plots
  • guided labs

An IDE or project workspace helps you see

  • files and folders
  • code and output
  • terminal commands
  • version-control changes

Agentic work is easier to review when the project has explicit structure.

Colab notebooks remain the lab format. This is not a demand that students adopt a particular IDE. The point is to know what files exist, what ran, and what changed.

Suggested pacing: 3 minutes.

[Sources] - /Users/aiwei/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Teaching/INST447/2025 Fall/Week 1 Introduction.pdf - /Users/aiwei/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Teaching/INST447/2026 Fall/week01_syllabus_v1.qmd [/Sources]

A reproducible analysis is a directed graph

Raw data
immutable → Clean + validate → Transform → Analyze → Figures · tables · report

If one input changes, you should know what must be rerun.

Explain “directed graph” in ordinary language: outputs depend on prior inputs. Raw data stays unchanged; cleaning and transformation steps are rerunnable. This makes debugging easier for both humans and agents.

Suggested pacing: 3 minutes.

[Sources] - /Users/aiwei/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Teaching/INST447/2025 Fall/Week 1 Introduction.pdf [/Sources]

Notebooks explore; scripts repeat

Notebook Script or function
Ask a question interactively Repeat a stable step
Inspect intermediate results Apply the same logic reliably
Combine explanation, code, and output Make dependencies easier to test
Easy to run out of order Usually runs from a defined entry point

Start by exploring. Move repeated logic into a form you can rerun and check.

Avoid claiming notebooks are “bad for AI.” The real problem is hidden state and out-of-order execution. Agents can work with either format, but explicit dependencies improve review.

Suggested pacing: 3 minutes.

[Sources] - /Users/aiwei/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Teaching/INST447/2025 Fall/Week 1 Introduction.pdf [/Sources]

A directory structure is external memory

project/
├── README.md          what this project does
├── data/
│   ├── raw/           unchanged inputs
│   └── processed/     reproducible outputs
├── notebooks/         exploration
├── src/               reusable code
├── output/            figures and tables
└── tests/             checks that should keep passing

Good names and boundaries reduce the amount that must live in your head.

This is an example, not a mandated template. The same principle applies to a small assignment: keep inputs, code, and outputs distinguishable. For an agent, the structure also communicates where it may safely work.

Suggested pacing: 3 minutes.

[Sources] - /Users/aiwei/Library/CloudStorage/Dropbox/Teaching/INST447/2025 Fall/Week 1 Introduction.pdf [/Sources]

The goal is not to type every line

The goal is to build a data workflow you can understand, inspect, rerun, check, and explain.

AI can accelerate the work. Those five verbs remain yours.

Close by resolving the elephant framing. We will use contemporary tools, but the course is still about trustworthy work with data. Preview next week: filtering and transformation.

A bit about my research

Wei Ai — research overview

Assistant Professor, INFO & UMIACS

Recent focus: AI for K-12 education

  • Using AI/LLM to help teachers in K-12 classrooms
  • Promoting high-quality instruction through automated feedback
  • Reducing teachers’ workload and enhancing lesson planning with AI tools

More broadly

Integrating heterogeneous expertise knowledge in behavior retrieval, measurement, and discovery

The data challenges in this work

  1. Multimodal and messy data — classroom video, audio, text, and structured records do not arrive clean
  2. Data scarcity, two kinds — not enough labeled examples, and not enough of the rare events that matter most
  3. Getting expertise out of the data we do have — translating what experienced teachers know into something a model can learn from
  4. Closing the loop with stakeholders — research that does not reach teachers and schools does not improve instruction

Optional bonus slide for students who are curious about the instructor’s research. Each challenge connects to themes in the course: messy data, scarcity, domain knowledge, and the gap between analysis and action. Keep it brief and conversational.

Suggested pacing: 3–5 minutes if time permits.
